g.text: SQL as a stream language — one addition, several consequences
TUMBLE(et) and TUMBLE(pt) disagree on 3 of 4 windows · 4 append-only rows vs 2 revised
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · TUMBLE(120s) gives 4 windows
THE SAME SQL, OVER A TABLE AND OVER A STREAM
one query text, two completely different execution models
over a finite TABLE
read 9 rows, emit 7 result rows, exit
over an unbounded STREAM
emit 7 rows so far, and keep running
so "the result" is
a table that changes, not a value that is returned
and the query's lifetime is
forever — there is no row count at which it is done
A batch query returns; a continuous query MAINTAINS. Everything else in this chapter follows from that one difference.
In particular, "when is the answer right?" becomes a question the query text has to answer, because nothing else will.
Step 1/4 — a query over a stream never finishes
The query text is identical and the execution model is not. Over a table it reads 9 rows and returns 7; over a stream it maintains those 7 rows
indefinitely. A batch query *returns*, a continuous query *maintains* — and that is why "when is this answer final?" has to be expressed in the
query rather than assumed.
SQL as a stream language — one addition, several consequences
TUMBLE(et) and TUMBLE(pt) disagree on 3 of 4 windows · 4 append-only rows vs 2 revised
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · TUMBLE(120s) gives 4 windows
THE MAPPING, WITH THIS DATASET
nothing new is invented; the relational algebra already has these
SELECT key, v
a transform — the "what" of ch02
WHERE v > 5
a filter — 4 of 9 rows: ids 2, 4, 6, 8
GROUP BY key
a keyed aggregation — 2 groups
GROUP BY key, TUMBLE(et, 120s)
keyed aggregation per WINDOW — 7 groups
The only row with no batch equivalent is the last: TUMBLE needs a TIME column, and batch SQL has no notion of event time.
So streaming SQL is not a new language. It is relational SQL plus one idea: a column whose values are a clock.
Step 2/4 — relational operations map straight onto streaming transforms
Three of these four rows are plain SQL doing plain SQL things. The fourth is the whole addition: `TUMBLE(et, ...)` requires a time column, and the
number of result groups jumps from 2 to 7 because the grouping key now includes a window. Streaming SQL is relational SQL plus a column that is a
clock.
SQL as a stream language — one addition, several consequences
TUMBLE(et) and TUMBLE(pt) disagree on 3 of 4 windows · 4 append-only rows vs 2 revised
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · TUMBLE(120s) gives 4 windows
TUMBLE ON et VERSUS TUMBLE ON pt
SELECT SUM(v) FROM clicks GROUP BY TUMBLE(et, INTERVAL '120' SECOND) — and the same query with pt
TUMBLE(et): 19 (ids 0,1,2,7)
TUMBLE(pt): 15 (ids 0,1,2)
DIFFERENT
TUMBLE(et): 11 (ids 3,6)
TUMBLE(pt): 2 (ids 3)
DIFFERENT
TUMBLE(et): 7 (ids 4,5)
TUMBLE(pt): 20 (ids 4,5,6,7)
DIFFERENT
TUMBLE(et): 8 (ids 8)
TUMBLE(pt): 8 (ids 8)
agrees
3 of the 4 windows get a different answer. One token in the query — `et` or `pt` — decides which.
And both are valid SQL producing valid results. Nothing in the engine can tell you the wrong one was chosen.
Step 3/4 — and the time attribute is a CHOICE with different answers
This is ch01's two-clock problem arriving as a one-token edit. `TUMBLE(et, ...)` and `TUMBLE(pt, ...)` differ by three characters and disagree on
3 of 4 windows — window [12:00, 12:02) reads 19 against 15. Both are valid SQL and the engine cannot flag either.
SQL as a stream language — one addition, several consequences
TUMBLE(et) and TUMBLE(pt) disagree on 3 of 4 windows · 4 append-only rows vs 2 revised
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · TUMBLE(120s) gives 4 windows
TWO QUERIES, TWO KINDS OF RESULT STREAM
the update mode is a property of the QUERY, not of the engine
SELECT * FROM clicks WHERE v > 5
APPEND-ONLY — 4 rows (ids 2, 4, 6, 8), none ever revised
SELECT key, SUM(v) FROM clicks GROUP BY key,…
UPDATING — 2 of 4 window rows get revised
window [12:00, 12:02) specifically
first 15, then 19 when id 7 arrives
what the sink must support
append-only: INSERT · updating: UPSERT, or a retraction
A filter can never revise a row — a row either matched or it did not. An aggregate over an open window can always be revised.
So you can read the update mode off the query text, and it tells you what the sink has to be capable of before you write any code.
Step 4/4 — so some results append and others UPDATE
The update mode is readable from the query, which makes it a design input rather than a surprise. A `WHERE` produces 4 facts that never change; a
windowed `GROUP BY` produces 4 rows of which 2 get revised — window [12:00, 12:02) goes 15 then 19. An INSERT-only sink is compatible with the
first and not the second.
